# **Introduction**

This report presents a process audit of a real Malaysian software product and compares it with our own experience of software development at USM. The organisation we selected is Prasarana Malaysia Berhad, the operator of the Rapid KL rail and bus network. Prasarana's main business is public transport, so we narrowed the audit to its software side: the **MyRapid PULSE** mobile application.

PULSE was first released in 2020 as a journey planner for Rapid KL, Rapid Penang and Rapid Kuantan services. Online ticketing was added in 2023, and on 1 May 2025 Prasarana replaced the app with a revamped version that added a cleaner interface, an "Explore City" feature and a rewards programme (Marketing-Interactive, 2025; Paul Tan's Automotive News, 2025). The app now offers a journey planner, a live bus tracker, a fare calculator and service alerts (Prasarana Malaysia Berhad, n.d.). We chose it because commuters depend on it every day, so a wrong arrival time is noticed immediately.

Prasarana does not publish its internal development process. Our audit is therefore based on public evidence: official announcements, app store listings, release notes and user reviews. Where we describe how the development team works, this is our inference from that evidence. For example, an App Store review reports that the bus times shown in the app did not match the actual departures (Figure 1), which suggests that defects are reaching users when they could have been caught earlier in the lifecycle.

For comparison, we use the Student Consultation and Appointment Booking System, developed for CCA103 System Analysis and Design (Semester II, 2025/2026) by a group that included three members of our current team: Lim Zhi Ying, Kung Ker Mian and Cecilia Se. The assignment required the group to analyse and design a web-based system that lets students book consultation slots with lecturers. It was delivered as two reports covering requirements, use case and UML models, a three-tier architecture, screen designs and a testing plan, across four modules: user identity and profile management, lecturer availability and slot management, booking and appointment coordination, and notification and feedback. The system was designed but not built, so in this report we treat it as a full project and extend it with implementation, test execution and release to students and lecturers.

The analysis is limited to the concepts covered in Weeks 2 to 6 of CKS222. Task 1 models a Code Review and Static Analysis activity in SPEM 2.0 and assigns responsibilities with a RACI matrix. Task 2 writes user stories and checks them with INVEST and Given-When-Then criteria. Task 3 designs a V-Model for verification and validation. Task 4 audits Lean wastes and aligns Extreme Programming practices. Task 5 tailors the process using Münch's 4 Ps and reflects on our team dynamics.
